course: Daily Broiler Sales: Batch Production System

lessons.title: Introduction and Why It Matters
lessons.body: Broiler chickens grow fast, but they are also fragile. A disease outbreak can wipe out your entire batch in days, turning your investment into a loss. In Africa, common killers include Newcastle disease, Gumboro (infectious bursal disease), coccidiosis, and chronic respiratory disease. These spread quickly through droppings, air, equipment, and even your clothes. Biosecurity is the set of simple, cheap actions you take every day to keep germs out and stop them from spreading if they get in. It is not about expensive drugs; it is about discipline. For example, a farmer in Kenya who lets visitors walk into the pen without boots can bring in Newcastle virus on their shoes. One week later, 80% of the birds may be dead. But a farmer who uses a footbath, keeps visitors out, and cleans drinkers daily can keep mortality under 5%. Healthy birds eat well, gain weight, and sell at top price. Sick birds eat less, grow slowly, and may be rejected by buyers. Your profit margin in broiler production is thinâoften only 10-15% per bird. One disease outbreak can erase profits for three batches. Biosecurity also protects your family and community from diseases like avian flu that can pass to humans. And it protects your reputation: buyers return to farms with consistent, healthy birds. The core rules are: keep a closed flock (no mixing with other poultry), clean and disinfect regularly, control traffic, and act fast when you see signs of illness. This module will give you the tools, steps, and habits to make biosecurity a normal part of your daily routine. You do not need a veterinary degreeâjust consistency and attention to detail.

lessons.title: Tools and Materials
lessons.body: To practice good biosecurity, you need a few basic tools and materials. Most are cheap and available in local agro-vet shops or markets. First, footbaths: use a shallow basin or a wooden box lined with plastic. Fill it with disinfectant solution. Common disinfectants include glutaraldehyde, quaternary ammonium, or bleach (sodium hypochlorite). Bleach is cheapest but loses strength in sunlight and dirtâchange it daily. A 0.5% bleach solution (5 ml bleach per 1 liter of water) works for footbaths. Second, boots: dedicated rubber boots that stay in the poultry house. Never wear them outside. Third, overalls or a farm coat: keep them inside the pen area. Fourth, hand washing: soap, water, and a nail brush. Fifth, cleaning tools: a stiff broom, a scraper, a high-pressure sprayer (or a knapsack sprayer), and scrubbing brushes. Sixth, disinfectants for surfaces: Virkon, glutaraldehyde, or a bleach solution (1% for surfaces). Seventh, rodent control: traps, bait stations, and wire mesh to block holes. Eighth, a foot-operated hand sanitizer station at the entrance. Ninth, a record book to track cleaning schedules, vaccinations, and any disease signs. Tenth, vaccines: keep a small cooler or fridge dedicated to vaccines (not food). Common vaccines in Africa: Newcastle (HB1, Lasota), Gumboro (intermediate), and fowl pox. Eleventh, a thermometer to check vaccine storage temperature (2-8Â°C). Twelfth, a spray bottle for spot disinfection. You also need a separate area for sick birds (hospital pen) with its own tools. Finally, a boot dip at the entrance of each pen, and a wheel dip for vehicles if you have a driveway. All these items cost less than the price of 10 birds, but they can save your whole batch. Buy them before you stock your next chicks.

lessons.title: Step by Step Method
lessons.body: Follow these steps daily to keep your broilers healthy. Step 1: Start with clean shoes and clothes. Before entering the poultry area, change into farm boots and overalls. Step 2: Use the footbath. Step into the footbath basin and scrub your boots on the brush provided. The disinfectant must cover the soles. Step 3: Wash hands with soap and water for at least 20 seconds. Step 4: Enter the pen. Walk calmly; avoid stressing the birds. Step 5: Check the birds first. Look for signs of illness: dull eyes, ruffled feathers, coughing, sneezing, watery droppings, or birds sitting apart. Count dead birds. Remove any dead birds immediately and dispose of them by burning or deep burial. Step 6: Check feed and water. Ensure feed is fresh and not moldy. Clean drinkers and refill with clean water. Add vitamins or electrolytes if birds are stressed. Step 7: Clean feeders and drinkers. Scrub them with a brush and disinfectant at least once daily. Step 8: Remove wet litter. Wet litter breeds coccidiosis and bacteria. Add fresh wood shavings or rice husks. Step 9: Check ventilation. Ammonia smell means poor air qualityâopen vents or curtains. Step 10: Record everything. Note mortality, feed intake, water intake, and any symptoms. Step 11: After working, clean tools and store them inside the pen area. Step 12: Before leaving, wash hands again and change back into street clothes. Step 13: Weekly, do a deep clean: remove all litter, scrub walls and floors with detergent, then disinfect. Step 14: Control visitors. Allow only essential visitors. They must wear farm boots and overalls, and walk through the footbath. Step 15: Vaccinate on schedule. Typical schedule: Newcastle at day 7 (HB1), day 21 (Lasota), Gumboro at day 14 and 21. Use clean water for oral vaccines. Step 16: Quarantine new birds for 2 weeks before mixing. Step 17: Set traps for rodents and repair holes. Step 18: If you see sick birds, isolate them immediately in a hospital pen and call a vet. Do not sell sick birds. These steps take 30-45 minutes daily but prevent disasters.

lessons.title: Common Mistakes and Fixes
lessons.body: Many farmers lose birds because of avoidable mistakes. Mistake 1: Not using a footbath. Fix: Place a footbath at every entrance. Use a lid to keep sunlight and rain out. Change disinfectant daily. Mistake 2: Wearing the same boots inside and outside. Fix: Keep dedicated boots inside the pen. Never wear them to the market or to visit other farms. Mistake 3: Allowing visitors without protection. Fix: Have spare boots and overalls for visitors. If they refuse, do not let them in. Mistake 4: Overcrowding. Fix: Broilers need space. Provide 10 birds per square meter (0.1 mÂ² per bird) for heavy breeds. Too many birds stress them and spread disease fast. Mistake 5: Wet litter. Fix: Stir litter daily and add fresh shavings. Fix leaking drinkers immediately. Mistake 6: Dirty drinkers. Fix: Wash drinkers daily with soap and disinfectant. Biofilm forms quickly and harbors germs. Mistake 7: Skipping vaccinations. Fix: Set phone reminders. Buy vaccines from reputable agro-vets and keep them cold. Mistake 8: Mixing age groups. Fix: Use separate pens for different batches. Never mix chicks with older birds. Mistake 9: Ignoring early signs. Fix: Act immediately. Isolate sick birds, increase vitamins, and consult a vet. Do not wait. Mistake 10: Using the wrong disinfectant. Fix: Use the correct dilution. Bleach for footbaths (0.5%), glutaraldehyde for surfaces (1%). Read labels. Mistake 11: Not cleaning feed storage. Fix: Keep feed in sealed containers off the floor. Clean up spills to avoid rodents. Mistake 12: Selling sick birds. Fix: Never sell sick birdsâthey spread disease and ruin your reputation. Bury or burn them. Mistake 13: No record keeping. Fix: Keep a simple notebook. Track mortality, feed, and treatments. This helps you spot problems early. Mistake 14: Poor personal hygiene. Fix: Wash hands before and after handling birds. Change clothes daily. Mistake 15: Ignoring wild birds. Fix: Cover openings with wire mesh. Wild birds carry diseases. Fix these mistakes and your flock will thrive.

lessons.title: Safety and Best Practice
lessons.body: Biosecurity protects your birds, but it also protects you and your workers. Always wear protective clothing: boots, overalls, and gloves when handling sick birds or cleaning. Wash hands thoroughly with soap after any contact with birds or their droppings. Some poultry diseases, like avian influenza and salmonellosis, can infect humans. If you have flu-like symptoms after handling sick birds, see a doctor and mention your work. When using disinfectants, follow safety rules. Bleach and glutaraldehyde can burn skin and eyes. Wear gloves and goggles. Mix in a well-ventilated area. Never mix bleach with ammoniaâit produces toxic gas. Store chemicals away from feed and out of reach of children. Vaccines must be stored correctly: keep them between 2-8Â°C. Do not freeze. Use a cooler with ice packs when transporting. Use clean, cool water for oral vaccines (no chlorine). Vaccinate in the cool part of the day. Handle birds gently to avoid stress. Dispose of dead birds properly: burn or bury deep (at least 1 meter) away from water sources. Never throw dead birds in the bush or river. This spreads disease. Keep a first-aid kit in the farm: soap, antiseptic, bandages, and eye wash. Train all workers on these practices. Post signs: 'No entry without boots' and 'Wash hands before entering.' Maintain a visitor log. Limit visits to essential people. Keep a closed flock: do not bring in birds from unknown sources. If you must, quarantine for 2 weeks. Keep the farm clean: remove weeds, standing water, and old equipment. Control rodents and insects. Use bait stations and fly traps. Best practice also means planning: have a vet's phone number, know the nearest diagnostic lab, and keep emergency funds for medicines. Finally, review your biosecurity plan monthly. Check what worked and what didn't. Adjust as needed. Healthy birds mean better profits and a safer farm for everyone.

lessons.title: Practical Exercise
lessons.body: Now it's time to put biosecurity into action. This exercise will help you set up a simple, effective system on your farm. You will need: a notebook, a pen, a footbath basin, disinfectant (bleach or glutaraldehyde), a scrubbing brush, rubber boots, overalls, soap, and a spray bottle. Step 1: Draw a map of your poultry area. Mark all entry pointsâdoors, windows, gates. Identify where you will place footbaths. You need one at each entrance. Step 2: Set up your footbath. Mix 0.5% bleach solution (5 ml bleach per 1 liter of water). Fill the basin so it covers the soles of your boots. Place a brush next to it. Step 3: Create a hand-washing station. Put a jerrycan with a tap, soap, and a nail brush near the entrance. Step 4: Prepare dedicated clothing. Hang overalls and boots inside the pen area. Make a rule: no one enters without them. Step 5: Do a daily check. For one week, follow the step-by-step method from Lesson 3. Record mortality, feed intake, water intake, and any symptoms in your notebook. Step 6: Clean and disinfect. On day 3 and day 7, do a deep clean: remove litter, scrub walls and floors with detergent, rinse, then spray with 1% bleach or glutaraldehyde. Let dry before adding new litter. Step 7: Check your vaccine schedule. Write down the dates for Newcastle and Gumboro vaccines. If you have chicks, vaccinate on time. Step 8: Control visitors. For one week, allow no visitors except essential workers. If someone must enter, they must wear farm boots and overalls and walk through the footbath. Step 9: Set up a hospital pen. Choose a small, separate area for sick birds. Keep separate feeders and drinkers. Step 10: Review your records. At the end of the week, calculate mortality rate: (number dead / number started) x 100. A good target is under 5% for broilers. If higher, find the cause. Step 11: Make a plan. Based on what you learned, write three improvements for next week. For example: 'Change footbath daily' or 'Fix leaking drinker.' Step 12: Share with a neighbor. Teach one other farmer these steps. Biosecurity works best when everyone in the area practices it. By the end of this exercise, you will have a working biosecurity system. Keep it up dailyâconsistency is the key to healthy birds and good profits.

quiz.q: What is the main purpose of biosecurity in broiler production?
options: A) To make birds grow faster
B) To keep diseases out and prevent their spread
quiz.explanation: Biosecurity focuses on preventing disease entry and spread, which indirectly supports growth and reduces losses.

quiz.q: Which disease is a common killer of broilers in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Newcastle disease is highly contagious and often fatal in poultry, including broilers.

quiz.q: What is a footbath used for?
options: B) Disinfecting boots before entering the pen
quiz.explanation: Footbaths disinfect boots to prevent carrying pathogens into the poultry house.

quiz.q: Which concentration of bleach is recommended for a footbath?
quiz.explanation: A 0.5% bleach solution is effective for footbaths and is safe when used correctly.

quiz.q: How often should footbath disinfectant be changed?
quiz.explanation: Disinfectant loses potency due to dirt and sunlight, so it should be changed daily.

quiz.q: What should you do with dead birds?
options: A) Sell them at a lower price
B) Throw them in the bush
C) Burn or bury them deep
D) Feed them to other animals
quiz.explanation: Proper disposal by burning or deep burial prevents disease spread to other birds and animals.

quiz.q: Which vaccine is commonly given at day 7 to broilers?
quiz.explanation: Newcastle HB1 is typically administered at day 7 as part of the vaccination schedule.

quiz.q: What is the recommended space per broiler in a deep litter system?
quiz.explanation: 10 birds per square meter (0.1 mÂ² per bird) is a common stocking density for broilers to reduce stress and disease.

quiz.q: Why is wet litter a problem?
options: A) It makes the pen look dirty
B) It breeds coccidiosis and bacteria
quiz.explanation: Wet litter creates a favorable environment for pathogens like coccidia and bacteria.

quiz.q: What should you do if you see a sick bird?
options: A) Ignore it, it will recover
B) Isolate it in a hospital pen
D) Mix it with healthy birds
quiz.explanation: Isolating sick birds prevents the spread of disease to the rest of the flock.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign of illness in broilers?
options: A) Active movement and loud chirping
B) Bright eyes and clean feathers
C) Ruffled feathers and dull eyes
quiz.explanation: Ruffled feathers and dull eyes are common indicators of illness in poultry.

quiz.q: What is the correct storage temperature for vaccines?
quiz.explanation: Vaccines must be kept refrigerated between 2-8Â°C to maintain potency.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid mixing different age groups of birds?
options: A) Older birds eat the younger ones' feed
B) Younger birds may carry diseases that older birds resist
quiz.explanation: Different age groups have different immunity levels; mixing can spread diseases from older carriers to younger susceptible birds.

quiz.q: What should you use to clean drinkers?
quiz.explanation: Soap and disinfectant remove biofilm and kill pathogens on drinkers.

quiz.q: How long should you quarantine new birds before mixing?
quiz.explanation: A 2-week quarantine allows time for any latent diseases to show before introducing new birds to the flock.

quiz.q: Which of these is a biosecurity tool?
quiz.explanation: Footbaths are essential biosecurity tools for disinfecting footwear.

quiz.q: What should you do before entering the poultry pen?
options: A) Change into farm boots and overalls
quiz.explanation: Wearing dedicated farm clothing prevents bringing pathogens into the pen.

quiz.q: Why is record keeping important in biosecurity?
options: A) It helps you spot disease trends early
B) It makes the farm look professional
C) It is required by law
D) It helps you sell birds
quiz.explanation: Records of mortality, feed, and symptoms help identify problems early and track improvements.

quiz.q: What is the target mortality rate for broilers?
quiz.explanation: A well-managed broiler flock should have a mortality rate below 5%.

quiz.q: Which disinfectant is commonly used for surfaces?
quiz.explanation: Glutaraldehyde is effective for disinfecting surfaces in poultry houses.

quiz.q: What should you do with visitors who refuse to wear farm boots?
options: B) Do not allow them into the pen
D) Ask them to stand at the door
quiz.explanation: Allowing visitors without proper footwear risks introducing diseases; it's safer to deny entry.

quiz.q: Why should you control rodents in the poultry house?
options: A) They eat feed and spread diseases
quiz.explanation: Rodents consume feed and can carry pathogens that infect birds.

quiz.q: What is the correct way to handle a vaccine?
options: A) Keep it cold and use clean water for oral vaccines
C) Leave it in the sun
quiz.explanation: Vaccines must be kept cold and administered with clean, non-chlorinated water to remain effective.

quiz.q: What should you do if you suspect avian influenza in your flock?
options: B) Report to veterinary authorities and isolate the flock
quiz.explanation: Avian influenza is a notifiable disease; reporting and isolation are critical to prevent spread.

quiz.q: Which of these is a good personal hygiene practice?
options: A) Washing hands after handling birds
B) Wearing the same clothes all week
quiz.explanation: Hand washing after contact with birds reduces the risk of spreading pathogens to yourself and others.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of a hospital pen?
quiz.explanation: A hospital pen separates sick birds to prevent disease transmission to healthy ones.

quiz.q: How often should you do a deep clean of the poultry house?
quiz.explanation: Weekly deep cleaning removes built-up organic matter and reduces pathogen load.

quiz.q: What should you do with feed spills?
options: A) Leave them for birds to eat later
quiz.explanation: Cleaning feed spills prevents attracting rodents and mold growth.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign of poor ventilation?
quiz.explanation: Ammonia buildup indicates poor air quality, which can damage respiratory health.

quiz.q: Why is it important to train workers on biosecurity?
options: A) To ensure everyone follows the same safe practices
C) To reduce the number of workers
D) To make them work faster
quiz.explanation: Consistent training ensures all workers understand and apply biosecurity measures correctly.
